entry.title: Upgrading a Long-Running Hobby Site from Drupal 10 to 11

link.title: Upgrading a Long-Running Hobby Site from Drupal 10 to 11

entry.content:
Background: Three Generations of Drupal Upgrades

I have maintained a long-running Drupal hobby site across several major versions: first upgrading from Drupal 7 to 9, later from Drupal 9 to 10, and most recently from Drupal 10.6 to 11.4.

Each transition had a very different engineering profile:

  • Drupal 7 → 9 took a significant amount of time. Because Drupal 8+ introduced a completely different architecture built on Symfony, Twig, and an entity/configuration system, moving off Drupal 7 was not an in-place upgrade—it required rebuilding the theme and running a full data and configuration migration.
  • Drupal 9 → 10 was much simpler by comparison, primarily involving deprecated API replacements and Composer dependency updates.
  • Drupal 10 → 11 (10.6.21 → 11.4.12) took just 2 days total from initial codebase audit and local Lando testing to production deployment.

Working with an AI coding agent during this upgrade compressed the timeline considerably. Before I ran a single Composer command, the agent audited all custom modules, theme templates, JavaScript libraries, and contributed module constraints, organized the work into a two-stage checklist, and flagged several subtle breaking changes that would have otherwise taken hours to debug manually.

What It Takes: An In-Place Upgrade

Unlike the Drupal 7 migration era, upgrading from Drupal 10 to Drupal 11 is a true in-place upgrade. All content, users, taxonomy terms, book outlines, and entity schemas remain in the existing database. The upgrade is executed through Composer package updates followed by drush updatedb and drush cr.

1. Environment & Database Prerequisites

Drupal 11 raises the minimum runtime requirements to PHP 8.3+ and MySQL 8.0+ / MariaDB 10.6+.

  • Production: My production server was already running PHP 8.4 and MariaDB 10.11, so no OS or database server upgrades were needed on the host.
  • Local Development (Lando): My local Lando environment was still configured with mysql:5.7 from an older recipe. Updating .lando.yml to use database: mysql:8.0 and importing a fresh production database dump aligned the local environment with Drupal 11’s requirements.

2. settings.php Updates for Drupal 11

To clear Drupal 11 status report warnings and follow current database best practices, three adjustments were added to sites/default/settings.php:

  1. Transaction Isolation Level (READ COMMITTED): Configured via init_commands on the database connection array to avoid unnecessary gap locks: 
    $databases['default']['default']['init_commands'] = [
  'isolation_level' => "SET SESSION transaction_isolation='READ-COMMITTED'",
];
  2. Explicit Database Driver Autoloading: Added the explicit Drupal\mysql\Driver\Database\mysql namespace and autoload path (core/modules/mysql/src/Driver/Database/mysql/).
  3. State Cache: Enabled $settings['state_cache'] = TRUE;, which Drupal 11 recommends for sites with a small state table to reduce database queries on every request.

Two-Stage Upgrade Strategy

Rather than jumping directly to Drupal 11 in a single Composer transaction, splitting the upgrade into two distinct stages kept dependency resolution predictable and allowed database update hooks to run cleanly.

Stage Target Core Key Actions
Stage A: Drupal 10 Prep 10.6.21 Transition removed core modules (book, tour), upgrade blocking contrib packages, update custom code for D11 compatibility
Stage B: Drupal 11 Upgrade 11.4.12 Upgrade drupal/core-*, drush/drush, Symfony 7.4, and add jQuery 4 compatibility for the legacy Bootstrap 4 theme

Stage A: Preparation on Drupal 10.6

  1. Handling Core Modules Removed in Drupal 11:
    • book module: Drupal 11 moved the core Book module to contrib (drupal/book). While still on Drupal 10.6, requiring drupal/book:^2.0 via Composer allowed the contributed module to take over existing book database tables and outlines without data loss.
    • tour module: The core Tour module was also removed in Drupal 11. Because the site did not use it, running drush pm:uninstall tour -y on Drupal 10 cleanly removed its configuration before upgrading core.
  2. Upgrading Blocking Contrib Packages:
    • Upgraded composer/installers (v1.12 → v2.3)
    • Upgraded drupal/field_validation (1.x → 3.0.0)
    • Upgraded drupal/google_cse (3.x → 5.0.6)
  3. Custom Module & Theme Compatibility:
    • Updated custom module and subtheme .info.yml files to core_version_requirement: ^10 || ^11.
    • Replaced the deprecated user_load_by_name() helper in custom form validation code (removed in Drupal 11) with the entity storage query: 
      $users = \Drupal::entityTypeManager()
  ->getStorage('user')
  ->loadByProperties(['name' => $entered_name]);
$account = reset($users);

Stage B: Upgrading Core to Drupal 11.4

With all contrib modules and custom code compatible with both Drupal 10 and 11, the core upgrade in composer.json was straightforward:

  • drupal/core-recommended, drupal/core-composer-scaffold, and drupal/core-project-message: 10.6.21 → 11.4.12 (bringing in Symfony 7.4)
  • drush/drush: ^12.5 → ^13.8
  • drupal/bootstrap_barrio: 5.5.20 → 5.5.22

Running composer update -W and drush updatedb -y completed the core schema and configuration updates cleanly.

Subtle Issues Caught Along the Way

Several non-obvious issues surfaced during local testing and deployment. Having an AI agent inspect the plugin definitions, display configurations, and browser console errors saved significant troubleshooting time.

1. drupal/book 2.0 Hid the Book Outline Navigation

After switching from the core book module to contrib drupal/book 2.0.x and running drush updatedb, the book navigation block at the bottom of book pages (the child page tree and previous/up/next links) disappeared.

Cause: drupal/book 2.0 converts the hardcoded book navigation into a configurable extra field (book_navigation) on the node entity view display, and its update hook places that component in the hidden region by default.

Fix: Re-enabling the book_navigation component on the node.book.default entity view display restored the bottom navigation immediately without modifying any Twig templates:

drush php:eval "
\$display = \Drupal::entityTypeManager()
  ->getStorage('entity_view_display')
  ->load('node.book.default');
\$display->setComponent('book_navigation', [
  'weight' => 100,
  'region' => 'content',
])->save();
"

2. drupal/field_validation 1.x → 3.0.0 (PluginNotFoundException)

Upgrading drupal/field_validation from 1.x to 3.0.0 initially failed during drush updatedb with:

Drupal\Component\Plugin\Exception\PluginNotFoundException: The "regex_field_validation_rule" plugin does not exist.

Cause: Version 3.0.0 renamed its core validation plugins and moved the legacy 1.x plugin IDs (regex_field_validation_rule, length_field_validation_rule) into a bundled field_validation_legacy submodule.

Fix: Enabling the legacy submodule (drush pm:enable field_validation_legacy -y) before running drush updatedb allowed existing field validation rule sets to continue working without recreating configuration.

3. jQuery 4.0 in Drupal 11 vs. Legacy Bootstrap 4 Theme

The site uses a custom subtheme based on bootstrap_barrio with Bootstrap 4.5.0. Upgrading to Drupal 11 broke interactive Bootstrap 4 components (such as modal dialogs) due to two separate changes:

  1. Missing core/jquery Dependency in bootstrap_barrio: Starting in bootstrap_barrio 5.5.20, the base theme dropped core/jquery from its global-styling library definition. On pages where no other module requested jQuery, bootstrap.min.js loaded without window.jQuery. Adding explicit core/jquery and core/drupal dependencies to the subtheme’s .libraries.yml ensured jQuery always loaded before Bootstrap.
  2. Bootstrap 4’s Hardcoded jQuery Version Check & Removed Helpers: Drupal 11 upgraded core jQuery from 3.7.1 to 4.0.0. Bootstrap 4.5.0 runs Util.jQueryDetection() on load, which checks the major version and throws: 
    TypeError: Bootstrap's JavaScript requires at least jQuery v1.9.1 but less than v4.0.0

    Additionally, Bootstrap 4 calls legacy jQuery utility methods ($.isArray, $.trim, $.camelCase) that were deprecated in jQuery 3 and removed in jQuery 4.0.

Fix: Rather than turning a 2-day core upgrade into a full Bootstrap 5 theme rewrite, we added an 18-line compatibility shim (jquery4-bootstrap4-compat.js) loaded immediately before bootstrap.min.js in the subtheme library:

(function ($) {
  'use strict';
  if (!$) return;

  if (typeof $.isArray !== 'function') {
    $.isArray = Array.isArray;
  }
  if (typeof $.trim !== 'function') {
    $.trim = function (text) {
      return text == null ? '' : (text + '').trim();
    };
  }
  if (typeof $.camelCase !== 'function') {
    $.camelCase = function (string) {
      return (string + '')
        .replace(/^-ms-/, 'ms-')
        .replace(/-([a-z])/g, function (_all, letter) {
          return letter.toUpperCase();
        });
    };
  }
  if ($.fn && $.fn.jquery && $.fn.jquery.indexOf('4.') === 0) {
    $.fn.jquery = '3.7.1-compat (' + $.fn.jquery + ')';
  }
})(window.jQuery);

This polyfilled the three removed functions and satisfied Bootstrap 4’s version check while keeping Drupal 11’s native jQuery 4 runtime intact.

4. Post-Deploy Cron & sites/default/files Ownership

Shortly after deploying to production, Drupal’s log reported a cron failure from the Feeds module:

RuntimeException: Feeds directory "public://feeds/in_progress/..." either cannot be created or is not writable.

Cause: The server’s user crontab was executing drush cron as the SSH user rather than the web server user (www-data). Whenever CLI cron created subdirectories inside sites/default/files/feeds, they were owned by the SSH user with 0755 permissions, preventing Apache (www-data) from writing to them on subsequent web requests.

Fix: Setting ownership of sites/default/files to www-data:www-data with the setgid bit (chmod 2775) and updating the crontab entry to run Drush as sudo -u www-data permanently prevented permission drift between CLI and web processes.

Production Deployment

Because all dependency conflicts and schema updates were validated locally against a copy of the production database first, the production cutover took less than 15 minutes:

# 1. Back up database and enable maintenance mode
drush sql:dump --gzip --result-file=~/backups/pre-d11-upgrade.sql
drush state:set system.maintenance_mode 1 --input-format=integer
drush cr

# 2. Pull two-stage commits and install production dependencies
git pull origin main
composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader

# 3. Apply database updates and disable maintenance mode
drush updatedb -y
drush cr
drush state:set system.maintenance_mode 0 --input-format=integer
drush cr

Key Takeaways

  1. Modern Drupal major upgrades are incremental: Unlike the Drupal 7 → 9 migration, upgrading from Drupal 10 to 11 is an in-place Composer and database update operation that can be completed in a weekend.
  2. Bridge Drupal 10 and 11 in two stages: Switching removed core modules (book, tour) and upgrading contrib blockers while still on Drupal 10.6 isolates module-level quirks (like field_validation_legacy and book_navigation) from the core upgrade itself.
  3. You don’t have to rewrite a Bootstrap 4 theme just for jQuery 4: A tiny compatibility shim for $.isArray, $.trim, $.camelCase, and $.fn.jquery lets legacy Bootstrap 4 JavaScript run smoothly on Drupal 11.
  4. AI agents excel at upgrade pre-flight checks: Having an agent cross-reference custom code, .info.yml files, library definitions, and contrib upgrade paths upfront turned what is normally a tedious manual audit into a predictable checklist.
entry.summary: A practical walkthrough of an in-place upgrade from Drupal 10.6 to 11.4 in two days—covering two-stage Composer preparation, Lando database updates, jQuery 4 compatibility with Bootstrap 4, and subtle contrib module breaking changes.

entry.title: Using Muse as a Coding Agent: From a VM Clone to a Merged Pull Request

link.title: Using Muse as a Coding Agent: From a VM Clone to a Merged Pull Request

entry.content:
Motivation: An Assistant With Its Own Computer

Most AI coding tools live inside your editor or your terminal. Muse (Meta’s personal AI agent) is different in one important way: it comes with its own Linux VM — a real shell, a browser, persistent storage. So I asked a simple question about Marginalia, my self-hosted RSS reader:

Can Muse act as a coding agent for this repo — clone it on its VM, build, test, push a branch, and open a pull request — while I only direct and review?

The alternative (read/edit access to a single folder on my Mac) has no shell behind it — no git, no Maven, no tests. I chose the VM clone.

One framing note for everything below: all terminal work happened inside Muse’s VM. I never typed those commands, and I didn’t see most of them at the time — I saw requests, results, and summaries in chat. The commands quoted in this post are reconstructed from Muse’s reports.

Setup: What I Asked vs. What Muse Figured Out

What I asked: clone this repo on your VM, and verify the build the way CI does.

What Muse did on its own:

  • Installed the matching JDK and verified both parts — the frontend passed immediately.
  • When Java’s network access was blocked, identified the exact Muse permission setting causing it and the single destination to allow (Maven Central), then waited for me to change it.
  • When the backend test run showed 26 failures out of 143, traced them to one cause: the VM’s DNS returns synthetic 198.18.0.0/15 addresses, which Marginalia’s SSRF validator blocks by design. Fixed it with a JVM-only hosts workaround — zero repository changes — and all 143 tests passed.
  • When GitHub SSH on port 22 timed out through the VM’s gateway, switched to SSH over port 443.

Rules I set before any real work (my only other setup input):

  1. Never push to main. Always a branch, with an agent-specific prefix.
  2. For UI changes, show me a visual before pushing.
  3. Agent commits must be distinguishable from mine: me as author, the agent in the committer field plus a Co-authored-by trailer. Muse first picked a committer address that turned out to belong to a real, unrelated GitHub user — it caught this itself via the API, switched to a local-only address that links to no account, and re-verified.

Who Does What: One-Time, Every Task, Automatic

The clearest way to summarize the whole experiment:

  What When
My intervention (one-time) Switch the network permission to “Ask” and approve Maven Central · Add Muse’s SSH key as a deploy key on this repo only · Connect the official GitHub connector (OAuth) and select marginalia only for the GitHub App Setup only — done once, reused by every future task
My intervention (every task) Describe the task and constraints · Approve the visual (for UI work) · Approve the merge · Deploy on my server (git pull + rebuild the frontend container) Per task
Automatic (Muse) Clone, toolchain setup, build, lint, tests · Branch, commit (with the identity scheme above), push · Screenshots for review · Open the PR, check CI status Per task, no input from me

The one-time items are done exactly once. After that, each task is the third row plus a few approvals from me.

The First Task: A Button My Thumb Can’t Reach

What I asked: on my iPhone 17 Pro, Marginalia’s article reader is full-screen and the only close control is a ~32 px X in the top-left corner. Evaluate first: (1) a button at the bottom, (2) a swipe gesture, or (3) something else.

What Muse figured out: it read the actual component, ruled out swipe-up (it conflicts with the reading scroll), pointed out that a footer button only helps at the end of an article, and recommended a fixed mobile bottom bar plus a 44 px close target.

What I decided: do bottom bar plus a 44 px close target — but show me the visual before any push.

Muse implemented it locally, rendered the real component in a browser at the phone’s viewport (402 × 874), and sent full-screen screenshots (at rest / mid-scroll / end of article). I approved, and it pushed the branch.

The change itself is one file — details are in the commit: the merged commit on main and PR #38.

Merging, as I asked: squash and merge, keeping the full commit message. Muse checked CI first (backend ✔, frontend ✔), merged through the connector, and afterwards I deployed with git pull + docker compose up -d --build caddy — frontend-only, a fact Muse confirmed from the compose file rather than assumed.

Creating the PR: Three Failed Approaches, Then the Working One

Pushing the branch took seconds. Opening the PR took much longer:

  1. Browser automation — hit GitHub’s sign-in wall; a full account session in an agent’s browser is broader access than I wanted to hand over. I stopped it.
  2. gh — installed but not logged in, and Muse’s vault deliberately never provides stored tokens to shell tools. So gh could not be used.
  3. A fine-grained token I pasted in chat — scoped to one repo, used exactly once to create PR #38, deleted by me right after. It worked, but a token in a chat log is not a pattern to repeat.
  4. The official GitHub connector — OAuth + the Muse GitHub App, with repository selection (marginalia only). No token exists anywhere. This was available from the start; neither of us checked the connector catalog first. Lesson recorded.

Open Question: What Else Is This VM For?

One thing I genuinely don’t know yet, and want to test next: how far does this VM generalize?

  • A different repository? Presumably yes — another clone, another deploy key, another line in the repo-selection list. Nothing in the setup was Marginalia-specific except the JDK version.
  • A different purpose entirely? For example, scheduled jobs: a script that runs every morning — checking CI status, watching a feed, compiling a report — and messages me only when something matters. The VM persists between conversations, which is exactly what scheduled work needs.

Both are unverified. If they work, the VM stops being “where the coding agent lives” and becomes a small always-on machine that happens to have an AI operator.

Key Takeaways

  1. The bottleneck was never code generation — it was setting up access permissions and verifying results. The one-time setup column above is where the time went.
  2. Constraints make autonomy reviewable: branch-only pushes, a distinct committer identity, and a screenshot approval step made supervision a few approvals.
  3. Use the narrowest credential that does the job. In increasing order of scope: repo-scoped deploy key < repo-scoped token < app installation on selected repos < full account session.
  4. “Tests are failing” ≠ “code is wrong” — here the sandbox DNS was returning incorrect addresses to the JVM, and the fix belonged to the environment, not the repo.
  5. Check the platform’s first-party options first. The official connector was more secure and less work than every workaround that preceded it.
entry.summary: Evaluating Meta's Muse agent inside a standalone Linux VM: repository cloning, SSRF test workarounds, mobile UI adjustments, and secure GitHub App workflows.

entry.title: Exploring Multi-Cloud Deployments: Migrating from AWS Lightsail to Oracle Cloud (OCI)

link.title: Exploring Multi-Cloud Deployments: Migrating from AWS Lightsail to Oracle Cloud (OCI)

entry.content:
Motivation: Beyond Single-Vendor Lock-In

When I built and deployed Marginalia—my private, self-hosted RSS reader web application—AWS Lightsail was the natural starting point. For $7.00/month, Lightsail provided a simple, self-contained VPS with a bundled static IP and firewall. Paired with Docker Compose and Caddy for automated Let’s Encrypt TLS, it worked reliably and without fuss.

However, relying entirely on a single cloud vendor introduces subtle technical trade-offs. As cloud offerings mature, different hyperscalers develop distinct strengths. For compute-heavy or persistent personal workloads, exploring alternative cloud providers—specifically Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) and its modern Ampere Altra ARM64 architecture—presented an exciting opportunity.

While cutting operational costs from ~$7/month to $0/month through OCI’s Always Free tier was a welcome catalyst, the true engineering objective was broader: architectural vendor neutrality.

I wanted Marginalia’s infrastructure to treat compute providers as interchangeable commodities. If AWS Lightsail, OCI, Hetzner, or a bare-metal server can run Docker, our Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and deployment workflows should support switching between them in minutes—without risking DNS misconfigurations or touching long-lived backup storage.

The Architecture: Decoupling Compute, Routing, and Backups

In monolithic Terraform repositories, compute instances, DNS records, and backup storage buckets often live inside the same main.tf and share a single state file.

This tight coupling is dangerous during cloud migrations: running terraform destroy to decommission an old server risks accidentally destroying your DNS zones or wiping out historical database backup buckets.

To achieve clean multi-vendor support, I restructured Marginalia’s deployment layout into four decoupled stacks, each with an independent lifecycle and isolated Terraform state:

deploy/terraform/
├── README.md                 # Architecture matrix & deployment quickstart
├── aws-lightsail/            # Compute Option 1: AWS Lightsail (~$7/mo)
├── oci/                      # Compute Option 2: Oracle Cloud ($0/mo Always Free ARM)
├── dns-route53/              # Independent Routing: Route 53 A-record pointer
└── backup-s3/                # Cross-Cloud DR: Encrypted S3 bucket & retention policy

1. Pure Provider Isolation

  • deploy/terraform/oci/ depends exclusively on oracle/oci. It has zero AWS dependencies and requires no dummy AWS credentials.
  • deploy/terraform/aws-lightsail/ depends exclusively on hashicorp/aws.
  • deploy/terraform/dns-route53/ is simply a routing pointer. It takes a generic target_ip variable (derived from whichever compute stack is active) and updates the subdomain A record.
  • deploy/terraform/backup-s3/ manages an encrypted, private S3 bucket with 90-day lifecycle retention. It remains 100% untouched whether compute is hosted on AWS, OCI, or elsewhere.

2. Zero Application Code Changes

Because Docker base images (Ubuntu, Eclipse Temurin Java 25, Node.js 22, Caddy, MySQL 8.4) publish multi-architecture manifests supporting both linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, the exact same compose.yaml, Caddyfile, environment configuration, and database scripts run identically on both AWS (x86_64) and OCI (ARM64).

3. Component & Technology Stack

Component Technology Role
Primary Cloud (Compute & Networking) Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Ampere Altra ARM64 compute (VM.Standard.A1.Flex), VCN, Reserved Static IPv4
Secondary Cloud (DNS & Disaster Recovery) Amazon Web Services (AWS) Route 53 (subdomain routing) & S3 (encrypted off-site backups)
Infrastructure as Code Terraform (v1.5+) Decoupled multi-provider stacks (aws-lightsail/, oci/, dns-route53/, backup-s3/)
Container Orchestration Docker Engine & Compose v2 Multi-arch container runtime (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64)
Reverse Proxy & TLS Caddy v2 Automated Let’s Encrypt ACME TLS, HTTP/3, and SPA static hosting
Application Stack Spring Boot 4.1 (Java 25) + React 19 + MySQL 8.4 Self-hosted RSS reader (Marginalia)

Cross-Cloud Resilience: The Real Win

By combining OCI and AWS, Marginalia now operates with true cross-cloud resilience:

flowchart TD
    User["Reader / Browser"] -->|HTTPS 443| Route53["AWS Route 53 (DNS)"]
    Route53 -->|A Record Pointer| OCIHost["OCI Compute (Ampere ARM64)"]

    subgraph "Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (Primary Host - $0/mo)"
        OCIHost --> Caddy["Caddy (Reverse Proxy & Auto TLS)"]
        Caddy --> Backend["Spring Boot 4.1 (Java 25)"]
        Backend --> DB["MySQL 8.4 Database"]
        Timer["systemd.timer (Daily 02:00 UTC)"] --> BackupScript["./backup.sh"]
        BackupScript --> DB
    end

    subgraph "Amazon Web Services<br/>(Disaster Recovery Storage)"
        BackupScript -.->|AWS CLI S3 Sync| S3Bucket["Private Encrypted S3 Bucket"]
    end
  • Compute & Ingestion: Handled by OCI’s high-performance Ampere Altra ARM64 instance (2 OCPUs, 12 GB RAM) at zero monthly cost.
  • Off-Site Disaster Recovery: Handled by AWS S3. Daily compressed database backups are automatically pushed to an encrypted S3 bucket with automated 90-day lifecycle expiration. Even in the worst-case scenario of an OCI tenancy loss, not a single feed subscription or article bookmark is lost.
  • Portability: If another cloud provider emerges in the future, adding a sibling directory under deploy/terraform/ (e.g. gcp-compute/ or hetzner/) requires only defining the VM and pointing dns-route53 to its IP.

Key Takeaways

  1. Multi-cloud isn’t just for large enterprises: With modular Terraform stacks and Docker containerization, even solo developers and personal open-source projects can achieve cloud vendor independence without excessive complexity.
  2. Decouple state early: Separating compute from long-lived assets (DNS, storage, IAM) eliminates migration friction and prevents costly accidental deletions.
  3. ARM64 is fully production-ready: Moving a modern Java 25 LTS (Spring Boot 4.1) backend and React 19 frontend from x86_64 to ARM64 was entirely seamless—zero code modifications, zero build issues, and flawless container parity.
  4. Resilience through diversification: Running compute on one cloud while keeping encrypted backups on another gives you enterprise-grade disaster recovery while taking advantage of the best pricing each vendor offers.

Appendix: The Migration Journey (Step-by-Step Operations)

For those interested in the operational mechanics, state surgery, and cutover commands, here is the detailed technical walkthrough.

Phase 1: Non-Destructive State Separation

Before touching any live infrastructure, I refactored the monolithic AWS state offline. Using terraform state mv, 10 existing AWS resources were split into the three new modular directories:

# Example: Moving Route 53 record into dns-route53 state
terraform state mv \
  -state=deploy/terraform/terraform.tfstate \
  -state-out=deploy/terraform/dns-route53/terraform.tfstate \
  aws_route53_record.marginalia aws_route53_record.marginalia

Running terraform plan on all three stacks afterward confirmed 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed—proving that the directory refactoring had zero impact on the live production server.

Phase 2: Building the OCI Infrastructure Stack

Next, I wrote deploy/terraform/oci/ to provision the new environment. Key technical solutions included:

  1. VCN & Security Lists: OCI requires provisioning a dedicated Virtual Cloud Network (VCN), Internet Gateway, Route Table, and Subnet. The Security List explicitly allows ingress for SSH (port 22), HTTP (port 80), and HTTPS (port 443 TCP/UDP).
  2. Host-Level iptables Rules: OCI’s official Ubuntu images include restrictive host iptables rules that drop incoming traffic on ports 80 and 443 by default, regardless of the VCN Security List. In user-data.sh.tftpl, cloud-init automatically inserts ACCEPT rules before the default Ubuntu REJECT rule: 
    iptables -I INPUT 6 -p tcp --dport 80 -m state --state NEW -j ACCEPT
iptables -I INPUT 6 -p tcp --dport 443 -m state --state NEW -j ACCEPT
netfilter-persistent save
  3. Dynamic Image Lookup: Rather than hardcoding image OCIDs (which change with every OS release), Terraform dynamically queries the latest Canonical Ubuntu 24.04 image matching the target architecture (aarch64 for Ampere ARM).
  4. Persistent Reserved Static IP: Allocated an Always Free Reserved Public IPv4 address (oci_core_public_ip) to ensure the host retains a fixed public IP across reboots and maintenance.

Phase 3: The Zero-Downtime Live Cutover

With the OCI instance provisioned and bootstrapped (Docker Engine, 2 GB swapfile, fail2ban), we performed the cutover:

  1. Pre-Staging: Cloned the repository to /opt/marginalia on the OCI host, copied deploy/.env, and pre-built the containers in parallel while the AWS Lightsail instance was still serving live traffic.
  2. Data Consistency: Paused the backend service on Lightsail to freeze database writes, generated a compressed database snapshot (marginalia_backup.sql.gz), transferred it to OCI, and restored it using ./deploy/restore.sh. All 2,508 articles, 16 feeds, 9 categories, and Flyway schema migrations were verified intact.
  3. DNS Repointing: Updated target_ip in deploy/terraform/dns-route53/terraform.tfvars from the Lightsail IP to the OCI Reserved Static IP and executed terraform apply.
  4. Automated TLS Issuance: Within 60 seconds of the DNS record propagating, Caddy on OCI automatically solved the ACME HTTP-01 challenge and obtained a fresh Let’s Encrypt TLS certificate for marginalia.nobudev7.com.
  5. Rollback Safety Net: Rather than immediately deleting the AWS Lightsail VM, it was left stopped but fully intact for a 24–48 hour observation window. If any subtle issue arose on ARM64, reverting a single line in dns-route53/terraform.tfvars would restore the entire AWS stack instantly.

entry.title: Building and Publishing c4002-python: A 24GHz mmWave Radar Driver for Raspberry Pi

link.title: Building and Publishing c4002-python: A 24GHz mmWave Radar Driver for Raspberry Pi

entry.content:
Open Source Links

  • GitHub Repository: github.com/nobudev7/c4002-python
  • PyPI Package: pypi.org/project/c4002-python/
  • Issue Tracker: github.com/nobudev7/c4002-python/issues

Technologies used

Component Technology Role
Hardware Raspberry Pi Host controller & UART interface
Sensor DFRobot C4002 (SEN0691) 24GHz FMCW mmWave human presence radar
Language Python 3.8+ Driver, CLI utilities, and telemetry decoder
Packaging Hatchling / pyproject.toml PEP 517/621 build backend
CI/CD & Release GitHub Actions + PyPI OIDC Automated testing, linting, and Trusted Publishing

Motivation

Traditional PIR (Passive Infrared) motion sensors are the standard choice for smart lighting and home automation, but they have a fundamental limitation: they only detect gross movement. If you sit still, a PIR sensor doesn’t report any movement.

To achieve true human presence detection, 24GHz millimeter-wave (mmWave) FMCW radar sensors work very well. They can detect micro-motions as subtle as human respiration and chest expansion up to 10 meters away.

Recently, I integrated the DFRobot C4002 (SEN0691) mmWave sensor into my Raspberry Pi home monitoring setup. However, while DFRobot provides an Arduino C++ library, there wasn’t a pip-installable Python package available for Linux and Raspberry Pi developers.

I decided to build c4002-python from the ground up, test it thoroughly on actual hardware, and publish it as an open-source package on PyPI and GitHub.

The Hardware: DFRobot C4002 (SEN0691)

The C4002 is a compact 24GHz FMCW radar module that operates between 3.6V and 5.5V with 3.3V TTL UART logic:

  • Micro-Motion & Static Presence: Detects sitting, breathing, or sleeping individuals up to 10 meters.
  • Motion Tracking: Measures target distance, speed, signal energy (0–100), and direction (Approaching vs Moving Away) up to 11 meters.
  • Ambient Light Sensor: Onboard photosensor rated for 0–50 Lux, useful for dusk-to-dawn lighting triggers.
  • Configurable Distance Gates: 80cm or 20cm resolution gates with customizable sensitivity thresholds.
  • Dual Output Modes: Standard 115200 baud UART protocol plus a digital OUT GPIO pin.

Wiring to Raspberry Pi

Connecting the C4002 to a Raspberry Pi’s 40-pin GPIO header requires only 4 or 5 jumper wires:

  Raspberry Pi GPIO Header                  DFRobot C4002
 ┌─────────────────────────┐               ┌─────────────┐
 │ Pin 2  [5V]             ├───────────────┤ VIN         │
 │ Pin 6  [GND]            ├───────────────┤ GND         │
 │ Pin 8  [GPIO 14 / TXD]  ├───────────────┤ RX          │
 │ Pin 10 [GPIO 15 / RXD]  ├───────────────┤ TX          │
 │ Pin 11 [GPIO 17]        ├───────────────┤ OUT (opt)   │
 └─────────────────────────┘               └─────────────┘

Decoding the 32-Byte Binary UART Protocol

The C4002 continuously streams 32-byte binary notification frames at 115200 baud. The frame layout is structured as follows:

  1. Header (4 bytes): Fixed synchronization pattern 0xFA 0xF5 0xAA 0xA5.
  2. Length (2 bytes, LE): Total packet length (0x0020 = 32 bytes).
  3. Control (2 bytes): Reserved byte 0x00 and message type (0x04 for Notification).
  4. Command ID (1 byte): 0x60 for live detection telemetry or 0x03 for background noise calibration status.
  5. Inner Payload:
    • Target Status (0 = No Target, 1 = Static Presence, 2 = Motion)
    • Ambient Light Intensity (uint16 LE, scale 0.1 Lux)
    • Active Distance Gate bitmask (uint32 LE)
    • Presence Disappearance Countdown (uint16 LE, seconds)
    • Presence Distance (uint16 LE cm) & Energy (uint8, 0–100)
    • Motion Distance (uint16 LE cm), Speed (signed int16 LE cm/s), Energy, and Direction
  6. Checksum (2 bytes, LE): 16-bit sum of all preceding bytes (sum(bytes[:-2]) & 0xFFFF).

Real-World Engineering Challenges

Building a production-ready driver required solving several practical hardware quirks:

1. Zero-Lag Hardware Synchronization

While using time.sleep() between reads was convenient at the beginning, it introduced serial buffer lag because the sensor streams telemetry continuously. For efficiency and real-time responsiveness, read_packet() blocks directly on the incoming UART stream until the next validated frame arrives:

# Paced directly by the sensor hardware clock
data = sensor.read_packet()

Letting the hardware clock pace the read loop eliminates buffer backlog and keeps CPU usage near zero.

2. Dark / Stealth Mode (Turning Off Onboard LEDs)

The C4002 module features two bright onboard LEDs: a blue RUN status LED and an OUT detection indicator. In a bedroom or office, the bright blue LED can be distracting.

By analyzing the module’s protocol command CMD_SET_LED_MODE = 0xA1, I implemented software-controllable LED states:

# Stealth mode: completely turn off both LEDs over UART
sensor.turn_off_leds()

# Or toggle them individually
sensor.set_run_led(False)
sensor.set_out_led(False)

Both example scripts also expose CLI flags (--led-off and --led-on) for instant toggling.

3. Automatic Background Noise Calibration

High-frequency 24GHz radar waves reflect off stationary room objects (metal cabinets, ceiling fans, moving curtains). The sensor includes a built-in background noise learning routine (CMD_ENV_CALIBRATION = 0x60). The library exposes:

sensor.start_env_calibration(delay_time=10, cont_time=30)

This gives you 10 seconds to exit the room, after which the sensor samples background reflections for 30 seconds and writes custom noise thresholds to prevent false triggers.

4. 1-Minute Windowed Time-Series Aggregation

Checking presence every 60 seconds directly risks missing transient events (e.g., someone walking through a room for 15 seconds). I added a windowed aggregator (examples/minute_aggregator.py) that continuously monitors the sensor at 1 Hz and exports 1-minute summaries (occupancy_pct, avg_distance_m, max_motion_energy, avg_light_lux) into CSV format, ready for Grafana or home dashboard charting.

Packaging and CI/CD Pipeline

To ensure the library is reliable and maintainable, I set up modern Python packaging and automation standards:

1. Modern Build System with pyproject.toml

Instead of legacy setup.py, the package uses PEP 517/621 with Hatchling:

  • Strict metadata and type hints.
  • Optional Raspberry Pi GPIO support via extra: pip install "c4002-python[gpio]".
  • Fast linting with Ruff configured to Python 3.8+ targets.

2. Multi-Version Testing on GitHub Actions

A GitHub Actions test workflow runs on every push and pull request, executing test suites across Python 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12 on Ubuntu runners using captured live sensor packet fixtures.

3. Publishing to PyPI via Trusted Publishers (OIDC)

Instead of storing permanent PyPI API tokens in GitHub repository secrets, c4002-python uses PyPI’s Trusted Publisher mechanism.

When a new version tag (e.g. v0.2.0) is published on GitHub, GitHub Actions generates an OpenID Connect (OIDC) cryptographic token. PyPI verifies the token directly against the repository identity (nobudev7/c4002-python) and workflow (publish.yml), building and publishing the source distribution (.tar.gz) and wheel (.whl) without any manual secrets.

Getting Started

Installation

Install directly from PyPI:

# Standard installation
pip install c4002-python

# With Raspberry Pi GPIO OUT pin support
pip install "c4002-python[gpio]"

Quick Example

from c4002 import C4002Sensor

# Connect to Raspberry Pi hardware UART (/dev/serial0)
with C4002Sensor(port="/dev/serial0") as sensor:
    # Optional: disable onboard LEDs for dark environments
    sensor.turn_off_leds()

    print("Monitoring presence. Press Ctrl+C to stop...")
    while True:
        data = sensor.read_packet()
        if data and not getattr(data, "is_calibrating", False):
            print(f"State: {data.target_state_name} | Light: {data.ambient_light_lux} Lux")
            if data.presence_detected:
                print(f"  Presence Distance : {data.presence_distance_m} m (Energy: {data.presence_energy}/100)")
                if data.motion_distance_m > 0:
                    print(f"  Motion Tracking   : {data.motion_distance_m} m at {data.motion_speed_m_s} m/s ({data.motion_direction_name})")

If you’re building a Raspberry Pi presence detection project, give it a spin and feel free to open an issue or pull request!

entry.title: PiLambdaChart: Building a Serverless IoT Dashboard with Raspberry Pi and AWS

link.title: PiLambdaChart: Building a Serverless IoT Dashboard with Raspberry Pi and AWS

entry.content:
Technology Role
Raspberry Pi Edge device (sensor host)
Python 3 (asyncio) Edge agent & sensor drivers
Java 21 Lambda chart generator
📊 JFreeChart Server-side chart rendering
AWS Lambda Serverless compute
DynamoDB Time-series & metadata storage
S3 Static file hosting
CloudFront CDN & HTTPS delivery
EventBridge Scheduled triggers
Terraform Infrastructure as Code
HTML / JS Frontend dashboard (vanilla, no framework)
CSS Styling & dark theme

I already had a serverless water level monitoring system running — a Raspberry Pi with an ultrasonic sensor uploading readings to DynamoDB, a Lambda function generating daily charts, and CloudFront serving them from S3. It worked well for that single purpose. But as I added more sensors — temperature, humidity, ambient light, motion — I realized the system was too tightly coupled to water level monitoring. The metric names, chart styles, and dashboard layout were all hardcoded for one use case. I wanted to rebuild it as a generic, multi-device telemetry platform that could handle any number of sensors and metrics, with a modern interactive UI — while preserving the serverless architecture that kept costs near zero.

Github Repo

The full project is open source: github.com/nobudev7/PiLambdaChart

The README walks through setting up each layer. If you have a Raspberry Pi with a DHT22 sensor and an AWS account, you can have a working dashboard in about an hour.

The Architecture

The system is split into four decoupled layers, each independently deployable and scalable:

  1. Edge (Raspberry Pi + Python) — An async Python daemon reads sensors at configurable intervals and writes readings to DynamoDB. Failed uploads are buffered in a memory-capped retry queue and flushed automatically when connectivity returns.

  2. Storage (DynamoDB) — Two tables: IoT_Telemetry for time-series data, IoT_Metadata for device and metric registries (names, units, chart types, icons). The telemetry table uses a composite partition key deviceId#metricId#year with an ISO-8601 timestamp as the sort key, which keeps partitions bounded and allows efficient daily range queries with a single BETWEEN operation.

  3. Processing (Lambda + EventBridge) — A Java 21 Lambda function triggered every 5 minutes by EventBridge. It queries a day’s worth of telemetry, renders dark-themed JFreeChart PNGs, generates JSON sidecar files for interactive tooltips, and uploads everything to S3.

  4. Frontend (S3 + CloudFront) — A pure client-side SPA (no build step, no framework) that fetches a catalog index and metadata JSON, then renders chart tiles, synchronized crosshairs, and a responsive dark-mode UI. CloudFront delivers it globally with HTTPS and optional HTTP Basic Auth.

Why Serverless

The decision to go fully serverless wasn’t academic — it was economic and operational.

With a traditional approach, I would need an EC2 instance (or at minimum a container) running 24/7 to receive sensor data and serve the dashboard. For a personal monitoring project, that’s $15-30/month in baseline costs plus the overhead of OS patching, uptime monitoring, and capacity planning.

With the serverless stack, the cost breakdown looks very different:

Component Cost Driver Typical Monthly Cost
DynamoDB On-demand reads/writes ~$0.25
Lambda 5-min invocations × 30 days ~$0.50
S3 Storage + requests ~$0.10
CloudFront Data transfer ~$0.50
EventBridge Scheduling Free tier

Total: ~$1.35/month — and zero servers to maintain. The infrastructure scales with usage, not with time.

The Edge: Sensors and Resilience

The edge agent supports multiple sensor types through a plugin architecture. Each sensor driver inherits from a BaseSensor class:

Sensor Interface Metric
DHT22 GPIO Temperature (°C), Humidity (%)
BH1750 I2C Ambient Light (Lux)
PIR GPIO interrupt Motion Count (triggers/min)
HC-SR04 Ultrasonic GPIO Water Level (cm)

One feature I found essential in practice was the retry queue. My basement Pi has intermittent WiFi, and without retry logic, data points were silently lost. The agent now buffers failed uploads in an asyncio.Queue with a configurable memory cap and automatically flushes them when connectivity is restored. In production, this has recovered hundreds of readings that would have otherwise been dropped.

The agent also auto-detects whether it’s running on actual Raspberry Pi hardware. When GPIO libraries aren’t available (e.g., on a Mac during development), it automatically falls back to simulated sensor data. This means the full pipeline can be tested end-to-end without physical hardware.

Chart Generation with JFreeChart on Lambda

As a Java developer, I naturally chose Java for the Lambda function. While looking for a charting library, I found JFreeChart — a mature, feature-rich library in the JVM ecosystem that produces publication-quality charts. It turned out to be an excellent fit for server-side rendering of dark-themed, styled chart images.

The chart generator renders dark-themed PNGs with a custom 8-color palette designed for high contrast against the slate background. Similar hues are spread apart across metric IDs so that adjacent metrics always have visually distinct colors:

Metric 1 → Sky Blue     Metric 5 → Purple
Metric 2 → Rose         Metric 6 → Teal
Metric 3 → Emerald      Metric 7 → Amber
Metric 4 → Orange       Metric 8 → Fuchsia

Alongside each PNG, the Lambda generates a JSON sidecar file containing the exact plot area boundaries and per-point data coordinates. This is the key to the frontend’s interactive crosshairs — the browser can calculate sub-pixel-accurate tooltip positions by mapping mouse coordinates onto the chart’s data space using these boundary values.

The Frontend: Zero Dependencies, Full Interactivity

The dashboard is a single-page application built with zero frameworks, zero build tools, and zero server-side rendering. The entire frontend is three files: index.html, style.css, and app.js.

On load, the browser fetches two files from S3:

  • file-list.json — a catalog of all available charts organized by device, metric, year, and month
  • metadata.json — device names, metric names, units, emoji icons, and chart configurations

From these, the app constructs the full sidebar navigation and chart tile grids entirely client-side. This means serving the dashboard costs essentially nothing — CloudFront delivers static files, and there is zero compute at view time.

The interactive features include:

  • Synchronized crosshairs across all metric charts for the same day
  • Data tooltips with time and value, snapped to the nearest data point
  • Full-screen lightbox for detailed chart inspection
  • Deep-linking via URL parameters (?device=1&year=2026&month=08&day=14)
  • Day-of-week color coding — Sunday in red, Saturday in blue

Infrastructure as Code

The entire AWS stack is defined in Terraform with feature flags for incremental deployment:

enable_lambda           = true
enable_cloudfront       = true
enable_metadata_seeding = true

This means you can deploy DynamoDB tables first, start collecting data, then add Lambda chart generation later, and finally enable CloudFront when you’re ready to go public. Each layer can be toggled independently.

Device and metric definitions live in terraform.tfvars (which is gitignored), keeping personal device names and locations out of the repository:

seeded_devices = {
  "1" = { name = "Sump Pump Monitor", location = "Basement" }
  "2" = { name = "Ambient Monitor",   location = "Bedroom" }
}

What I Learned

Building PiLambdaChart reinforced a few principles:

Event-driven architectures are naturally resilient. Each component — edge agent, DynamoDB, Lambda, S3, CloudFront — operates independently. If Lambda fails, the data is still in DynamoDB waiting. If the edge goes offline, the retry queue catches it. There’s no single point of failure.

Pre-rendered assets beat real-time rendering for dashboards. By generating charts as static PNGs on a schedule rather than rendering them in the browser on each page load, the dashboard loads instantly from a CDN cache. The JSON sidecar approach gives us the best of both worlds — static delivery with interactive overlays.

Serverless doesn’t mean simple. The infrastructure has real complexity: IAM least-privilege policies, DynamoDB partition key design, CloudFront cache behaviors, and Terraform state management. But that complexity lives in the infrastructure definition, not in day-to-day operational burden. Compared to running your own server, there’s much less to worry about — no OS patching, no uptime monitoring, no capacity planning.
entry.summary: Technology Role Raspberry Pi Edge device (sensor host) Python 3 (asyncio) Edge agent & sensor drivers Java 21 Lambda chart generator 📊 JFreeChart Server-side chart rendering AWS Lambda Serverless compute DynamoDB Time-series & metadata storage S3 Static file hosting CloudFront CDN & HTTPS delivery EventBridge Scheduled triggers Terraform Infrastructure as Code HTML / JS Frontend dashboard (vanilla, no framework) CSS Styling & dark theme

entry.title: Setting up Raspberry Pi with an Ultrasonic Sensor

link.title: Setting up Raspberry Pi with an Ultrasonic Sensor

entry.content:
This post explains how to build a water level gauge using a Raspberry Pi Zero W and an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor. While this is a well-established application for distance measurement, I am tailoring it specifically for monitoring sump water levels.

Background

I decided to rebuild my ultrasonic water level measurement system because my previous setup was aging and starting to produce inconsistent results. While I wasn’t certain if the sensor itself was the cause, a fresh start allowed me to modernize the entire stack.

Another goal was to update my Raspberry Pi OS and Python version. This ensures I can use recent libraries, such as AWS Boto3, without worrying about version compatibility issues.

Finally, I have been using version 1 of Raspi-Sump. While it has been a great tool, its philosophy is to handle most processing locally on the Pi. As I shift toward a “cloud-native” style utilizing AWS, I want to keep the software on the Pi side as lightweight as possible.

The Ultrasonic Sensor

I chose the HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor. It doesn’t measure distance directly; instead, the Raspberry Pi measures the duration from the moment a pulse is emitted to the moment an echo is detected. The distance is then calculated using the speed of sound (divided by two to account for the round trip).

There is a ready-made Python library called pinsource that handles this logic, including optional temperature adjustment. https://github.com/alaudet/pinsource

pinsource is easy to use because it abstracts away the detailed timing and multiple sampling. Its distance call returns the value in centimeters. By default, it takes 11 samples and uses the median result, which helps reduce measurement errors.

Pi Wiring

Because the HC-SR04 operates at 5V and the Pi’s GPIO pins take 3.3V, I used a voltage divider on the Echo pin. I used 1kΩ and 2kΩ resistors to safely step down the voltage. Other combinations work as well; for instance, a pair of 470Ω and 1kΩ resistors is also a common choice.

The following table shows the connections between the sensor and the Raspberry Pi:

HC-SR04 Raspberry Pi Function
VCC Pin 2 (5V) Power
TRIG Pin 5 (GPIO 3) Trigger Output
ECHO Pin 8 (GPIO 14) through voltage divider Echo Input
GND Pin 39 (Ground) Ground

Software Setup

First, install the prerequisites for the Linuxnorth library:

# 1. Import the signing key
curl -fsSL https://apt.linuxnorth.org/public_key.asc \
  | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/linuxnorth-archive-keyring.gpg

# 2. Add the repository
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/linuxnorth-archive-keyring.gpg] \
  https://apt.linuxnorth.org trixie main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/linuxnorth.list

Now, install pinsource:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3-pinsource

The library includes a CLI tool that can test if the sensor is working, providing output in both inches and centimeters:

$ pinsource -t 3 -e 14
trig pin = gpio 3
echo pin = gpio 14
speed = 0.1
samples = 11

The imperial distance is 23.0 inches.
The metric distance is 58.4 centimetres.

Sump Setup

To ensure accurate measurements, I created a “stilling well” using a 3-inch diameter PVC pipe. This guides the ultrasound pulse directly to the water in the sump and prevents it from picking up reflections from the water pump. Since the pump is often positioned above the water level, it can reflect the signal prematurely, causing the sensor to consistently report the distance to the pump rather than the water.

In my previous testing, 2-inch diameter PVC barely fits with old HC-SR04, and the new HC-SR04 I recently bought has slightly larger sensors and no longer fits. 3-inch diameter works with the sensor size and also reduce erroneous measurement.
entry.summary: This post explains how to build a water level gauge using a Raspberry Pi Zero W and an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor. While this is a well-established application for distance measurement, I am tailoring it specifically for monitoring sump water levels.

entry.title: Using an IR Sensor for Precise Distance Measurement on Raspberry Pi

link.title: Using an IR Sensor for Precise Distance Measurement on Raspberry Pi

entry.content:
Background

For the past five years, I have relied on the HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor. While it served its purpose well, it occasionally reported incorrect distances. I suspected this was due to its wide beam angle (directionality), which might have been picking up a nearby water pump when the water level was low. To mitigate this, I used a PVC pipe and mounted the sensor at the top to guide the signal.

Recently, however, these errors have become more frequent. The sensor often reports a distance of 0, which suggests it is either failing to receive an echo or experiencing crosstalk. To find a more robust solution, I decided to try out a Time-of-Flight (ToF) IR distance sensor, which should offer better precision and narrower directionality.

The Sensor: VL53L0X

I chose VL53L0X. It is a Time-of-Flight (ToF) laser-ranging sensor that measures distance by timing how long light takes to bounce off an object. Unlike standard IR sensors that rely on reflected light intensity, this method is less affected by a target’s color or reflectance.

Connecting to Pi

Wiring the VL53L0X to a Raspberry Pi Zero W is straightforward as it uses the I2C interface. Connect the four main pins on the sensor to the corresponding pins on the Pi’s GPIO header:

VL53L0X Pin Raspberry Pi Pin (Physical) Function
VIN Pin 1 (3.3V) Power
GND Pin 6 (GND) Ground
SCL Pin 5 (SCL / GPIO 3) I2C Clock
SDA Pin 3 (SDA / GPIO 2) I2C Data

Ensure your connections are secure before powering on the Pi. If your sensor breakout board has additional pins like XSHUT or GPIO1, you can leave them disconnected for a basic setup.

Enable I2C on Your Raspberry Pi

Since the VL53L0X communicates via the I2C protocol, you must enable I2C in the system configuration.

  1. Run the configuration tool: 
    sudo raspi-config
  2. Navigate to Interface Options and enable I2C.
  3. Reboot your Raspberry Pi for the changes to take effect.

Set Up the Library

Install pip3

If you haven’t installed pip3 yet, run:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3-pip

Adafruit CircuitPython Library

Attempting to install the Adafruit CircuitPython library system-wide may result in an externally-managed-environment error:

error: externally-managed-environment

× This environment is externally managed
╰─> To install Python packages system-wide, try apt install
    python3-xyz, where xyz is the package you are trying to
    install.
    
    If you wish to install a non-Debian-packaged Python package,
    create a virtual environment using python3 -m venv path/to/venv.

To resolve this, create and use a virtual environment as recommended:

python3 -m venv adaenv
source adaenv/bin/activate

Now, install the Adafruit VL53L0X library:

pip3 install adafruit-circuitpython-vl53l0x

Python Script to Measure Distance

Create a test script named measure.py to verify the sensor is working.

measure.py

import time
import board
import busio
import adafruit_vl53l0x

# Initialize I2C bus using the Pi's default SCL and SDA pins
i2c = busio.I2C(board.SCL, board.SDA)

# Initialize the VL53L0X distance sensor
try:
    sensor = adafruit_vl53l0x.VL53L0X(i2c)
    print("VL53L0X sensor detected successfully!")
except ValueError:
    print("Error: Could not find the sensor. Check your I2C wiring.")
    exit()

# Optional: Increase timing budget for higher accuracy (default is 33ms)
# Increasing this can improve precision at the cost of slower updates.
sensor.measurement_timing_budget = 200000  # 200ms budget

print("Starting distance measurements. Press Ctrl+C to stop.\n")

try:
    while True:
        # Read distance in millimeters
        distance_mm = sensor.range
        
        # Convert to centimeters
        distance_cm = distance_mm / 10.0
        
        print(f"Distance: {distance_mm} mm ({distance_cm:.1f} cm)")
        
        # Wait 0.5 seconds before the next reading
        time.sleep(0.5)

except KeyboardInterrupt:
    print("\nMeasurement stopped by user.")

Test Run

Execute the script within your virtual environment:

python3 measure.py

Output:

VL53L0X sensor detected successfully!
Starting distance measurements. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

Distance: 323 mm (32.3 cm)
Distance: 321 mm (32.1 cm)
Distance: 325 mm (32.5 cm)
Distance: 326 mm (32.6 cm)
^C
Measurement stopped by user.

Update

While the VL53L0X provides more accurate measurements in a clear path, it ultimately proved unsuitable for my sump water level application. I had hoped its narrower beam would avoid internal obstacles, but it still picked up reflections from the water pump rather than the water surface.

I have since returned to using an ultrasonic sensor, but this time with a “stilling well” to stabilize and isolate the readings. An IR sensor would likely work with a stilling well as well; I chose the ultrasonic sensor simply because I happened to have a new Pi and sensor already set up in a nice enclosure. See my later post for more details.
entry.summary: Background For the past five years, I have relied on the HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor. While it served its purpose well, it occasionally reported incorrect distances. I suspected this was due to its wide beam angle (directionality), which might have been picking up a nearby water pump when the water level was low. To mitigate this, I used a PVC pipe and mounted the sensor at the top to guide the signal.

entry.title: Deploying The Java Chart Generator To Aws Lambda On Schedule

link.title: Deploying The Java Chart Generator To Aws Lambda On Schedule

entry.content:
This blog post provides a minimal, step-by-step procedure for deploying the ChartGeneratorLambdaFunction Java JAR as an AWS Lambda function and scheduling it to run every 5 minutes.

Every 5 minutes is enough to generate up-to-date chart, although data points are uploaded every minute. If AWS cost is not a question, it can be every minute, or the lambda function can be run by each data point upload to DynamoDB.

The system design idea is described in my previous post - Migrating To Serverless: Raspberry Pi To Dynamodb Plus Lambda Function For Chart Generation

1. Build the Deployment Package

Compile the “fat JAR” containing all dependencies:

mvn clean package

Result: target/ChartGeneratorLambdaFunction-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar

2. Create the Lambda Function

  1. Open the AWS Lambda Console.
  2. Click Create function > Author from scratch.
  3. Function name: ChartGenerator (or your preferred name).
  4. Runtime: Java 21.
  5. (Optional) Architecture: Turn on ARM64 architecture.

3. Upload to S3 and Configure Lambda

AWS suggests to use S3 for files larger than 10MB. Because the Chart Generator JAR is 17MB, it is best to upload via S3:

  1. Upload to S3:
    • Go to your S3 bucket (e.g., chart-generator).
    • Upload target/ChartGeneratorLambdaFunction-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar.
    • Copy the S3 URI (e.g., s3://chart-generator/ChartGeneratorLambdaFunction-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar).
  2. Configure Lambda:
    • In the Code tab, click Update > Update from a file in Amazon S3.
    • Paste the S3 URI you copied.
    • In Runtime settings, click Edit and set the Handler to: com.nobudev7.ChartGeneratorHandler::handleRequest
  3. Configure Timezone The current set up is assuming that the data point is using local time zone for the data point. To make the JAR runs on the same time zone as RaspberryPi (although, this is a Sump Pump application constraint), set the Java time zone for the lambda function.
    • Open Configuration tab.
    • Navigate to Environment variables from the left panel.
    • Click Edit to add an environment variable.
    • Set JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS for Key, and set -Duser.timezone=<TIME_ZONE_STRING> for the value. For example, -Duser.timezone=America/New_York.
    • Click Save.

4. Configure IAM Permissions

The Lambda function must be authorized to read from DynamoDB and write to S3. Follow these steps to attach the necessary permissions:

  1. Navigate to Permissions: In the Lambda function console, click on the Configuration tab and select Permissions from the left-hand menu.
  2. Access the Role: Click on the link under Role name (e.g., ChartGenerator-role-xxxx). This will open the IAM Console in a new tab.
  3. Create Inline Policy:
    • In the IAM Console, click Add permissions on the right side and select Create inline policy.
    • Switch to the JSON editor tab.
  4. Apply the Policy: Paste the following JSON block, replacing <REGION>, <ACCOUNT_ID>, and <BUCKET_NAME> with your actual values:
{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "DynamoDBRead",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "dynamodb:Query"
            ],
            "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:<YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID>:table/Sump_Water_Level"
        },
        {
            "Sid": "LambdaCodeRead",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "s3:GetObject"
            ],
            "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::sump-chart-generator/*"
        },
        {
            "Sid": "ChartOutputWrite",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "s3:PutObject",
                "s3:GetObject"
            ],
            "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::sump-water-level/output/*"
        }
    ]
}

5. Adjust Resources

JFreeChart requires sufficient memory and time for image processing:

  • Memory: 512 MB to 384 MB.
  • Timeout: 30 seconds.

6. Schedule Execution

  1. Click Add trigger > EventBridge (CloudWatch Events).
  2. Select Create a new rule.
  3. Rule type: Schedule expression.
  4. Schedule expression: rate(5 minutes).
  5. Click Add.

7. Verify and Monitor Execution

To confirm your Lambda is running every 5 minutes, you can check the AWS CloudWatch Logs:

  1. Monitor Tab: In the Lambda console, click the Monitor tab at the top.
  2. View CloudWatch Logs: Click the View CloudWatch logs button. This opens the CloudWatch console in a new tab.
  3. Log Streams: You will see a list of Log streams. Each time the Lambda container starts or runs, it logs to these streams.
  4. Check Timestamps: Open the latest log stream. You should see entries like START RequestId: ... and END RequestId: ....
    • Verify that the Event time for these entries occurs every 5 minutes.
    • Look for the output from the Java code (e.g., Processing data for date: ...) to ensure the logic is executing successfully.
  5. Troubleshooting: If you don’t see logs or see ERROR entries, check the logs for specific Java exceptions (like AccessDeniedException if IAM permissions are wrong).
entry.summary: This blog post provides a minimal, step-by-step procedure for deploying the ChartGeneratorLambdaFunction Java JAR as an AWS Lambda function and scheduling it to run every 5 minutes.

entry.title: Migrating To Serverless: Raspberry Pi To Dynamodb Plus Lambda Function For Chart Generation

link.title: Migrating To Serverless: Raspberry Pi To Dynamodb Plus Lambda Function For Chart Generation

entry.content:
Building on the foundation of SumpDataVisualizerCli—my original Java tool designed to generate chart images from local CSV files—I’ve spent this week evolving the project into a fully automated, cloud-native solution. The goal was to take that local visualization logic and migrate it to AWS Lambda, transforming a manual process into a seamless serverless pipeline that handles everything from data ingestion to chart delivery. In this post, I’ll walk through how I bridged the gap between a Raspberry Pi and the AWS cloud to create a robust, hands-off monitoring system.

The Vision: Automated Peace of Mind

The goal was simple - generate water level charts automatically continuously. The system follows a clean, serverless flow:

  1. Data Collection: A Raspberry Pi reads water levels and pushes them to AWS DynamoDB.
  2. Storage: AWS DynamoDB acts as the high-performance, persistent data store.
  3. Visualization: An AWS Lambda function triggers upon data point upload, generate a PNG chart using JFreeChart, and serve it via Amazon S3.

The Architecture: Java in AWS Lambda

The core of the system is a Lambda function written in Java 21. It utilizes the JFreeChart library to handle chart generation. Because AWS Lambda has limited filesystem access and is designed for stateless execution, the code is optimized for in-memory processing:

See the code in this GitHub repo - ChartGeneratorLambdaFunction.

  1. Data Retrieval: The function queries DynamoDB for a specific date’s data points.
  2. In-Memory Generation: Instead of writing to a temporary file, the chart is generated and stored in memory as a byte[].
  3. S3 Stream: The byte array is then uploaded directly to an S3 bucket with the appropriate Cache-Control headers.

This approach keeps the function lightweight and avoids the overhead of managing local disk space during execution.

The Data Pulse: Raspberry Pi Ingestion

The “eyes and ears” of the project remain on-premises. A Raspberry Pi is responsible for the actual data collection. During this session, I developed two specialized Python scripts to ensure the data in my <TABLE_NAME> DynamoDB table is both timely and accurate.

1. Real-Time Heartbeat (upload.py)

This script runs every minute via a cron job. It captures the current date, time, and water level, then pushes a single data point to AWS. This gives us a “near-real-time” view of the sump activity.

2. The Fail-Safe Batch (batch_upload.py)

My home access point occasionally drops the WiFi connection, and standard minute-by-minute uploads might miss some data point. Also, because I run per-minute upload script using cron with some intentional delay to make sure the measurement is done, there’s always a missing “final minute” of a day’s dataset. To solve this, I created batch_upload.py that upload all data points from the prior day.

This script is designed to run shortly after midnight. It reads a full day’s worth of data from a local CSV file and performs a bulk upload. I implemented a specific rate-limiting strategy here: it writes in batches of 20 items with a mandatory one-second delay between each batch. The one-second rate limit ensures that it doesn’t go over the Write Capacity Unit (WCU) allowance under the DynamoDB free tier quota.

Bridging the Gap: Setting Up the Raspberry Pi

One of the highlights of this session was addressing the unique constraints of older hardware. My Raspberry Pi is running Raspbian Buster (Python 3.7), which presents some challenges for modern libraries.

Here is the approach I took to get boto3 (the AWS SDK for Python) running smoothly:

Environment and Versioning

Since boto3 version 1.30.0 dropped support for Python 3.7, I had to be surgical with my installation. I set up a dedicated virtual environment to keep the system clean:

# Create a dedicated workspace
mkdir aws-sump
cd aws-sump

# Set up the virtual environment
python3 -m venv myenv
source myenv/bin/activate

# Install a compatible version of boto3
pip3 install 'boto3<1.30.0'

Although the installation was successful, I got this warning.

s3transfer 0.8.2 has requirement botocore<2.0a.0,>=1.33.2, but you'll have botocore 1.32.7 which is incompatible.

Despite the warning about s3transfer dependencies, the core DynamoDB functionality works perfectly for my needs, so I figured it’s OK.

I then configured the local credentials at ~/.aws/credentials:

[default]
aws_access_key_id = <YOUR_ACCESS_KEY_ID>
aws_secret_access_key = <YOUR_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY>

Security First: IAM Policy

Following the principle of least privilege, I created a custom IAM policy for the Raspberry Pi user. This ensures that even if the Pi were compromised, the credentials only allow writing to the specific water level table:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "dynamodb:PutItem",
                "dynamodb:UpdateItem",
                "dynamodb:BatchWriteItem"
            ],
            "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:<YOUR_REGION>:<YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID>:table/<TABLE_NAME>"
        }
    ]
}

Conclusion

This is a part of migration to a serverless system - data point upload and chart generation. By using the power of AWS Lambda and DynamoDB, I’ve created basis of a monitoring system that is both resilient and serverless.

In this post, I’ll walk through how I bridged the gap between a Raspberry Pi and the AWS cloud to create a robust, hands-off monitoring system.

entry.title: Securing Serverless Site Migrating From S3 Hosting To Amazon Cloudfront Https

link.title: Securing Serverless Site Migrating From S3 Hosting To Amazon Cloudfront Https

entry.content:
Building a static site is easy, but making it professional and secure requires moving beyond basic S3 hosting. As part of my AWS Serverless Sump Chart project, I recently migrated my site to a CloudFront-driven architecture to support HTTPS and a custom domain. Here is the breakdown of how I structured the setup and the critical “gotchas” I discovered along the way.

Architecture

The setup follows a secure, serverless pattern:

User → HTTPS → CloudFront → OAC → S3 Bucket (Private)

In this configuration, S3 is no longer acting as a web server; it functions purely as private storage. CloudFront handles the heavy lifting of security, SSL termination, and content delivery.

Implementation Steps

  1. Request SSL Certificate: I used AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to obtain a free SSL certificate. Note that for CloudFront usage, the certificate must be requested in the us-east-1 (N. Virginia) region.
  2. Configure S3 Storage: I used my existing S3 bucket containing the website files. I ensured “Block Public Access” was enabled to keep the data private from the open web.
  3. Create CloudFront Distribution: I set up a new distribution and selected the S3 bucket as the origin.
  4. Implement Origin Access Control (OAC): This is the modern way to secure the connection between CloudFront and S3. It ensures that users cannot bypass CloudFront to access your files directly.
  5. Apply Bucket Policy: To allow CloudFront to fetch files from my private bucket, I applied a specific policy that grants s3:GetObject permissions only to my specific CloudFront distribution ARN. 
    {
    "Version": "2008-10-17",
    "Id": "PolicyForCloudFrontPrivateContent",
    "Statement": [
  {
      "Sid": "AllowCloudFrontServicePrincipal",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
          "Service": "cloudfront.amazonaws.com"
      },
      "Action": "s3:GetObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::sump-water-level/*",
      "Condition": {
          "StringEquals": {
              "AWS:SourceArn": ""
          }
      }
  }
    ]
}

Key Lessons

While standard tutorials cover the basics, these specific steps were crucial for a working production environment:

  • Disable S3 Static Website Hosting: Once you move to CloudFront with OAC, you should disable the “Static Website Hosting” feature in the S3 properties. Since S3 is now just a storage layer, leaving hosting enabled creates an unnecessary (and unencrypted) public endpoint.
  • Set the Default Root Object: This is the most common reason for a “403 Forbidden” or “Access Denied” error. Because CloudFront is fetching from a storage bucket rather than a web server, it doesn’t know to look for index.html automatically. You must manually define index.html as the Default Root Object in your CloudFront settings.
  • Redirect HTTP to HTTPS: To ensure a seamless user experience, I configured the CloudFront distribution behavior “Viewer Protocol Policy” to automatically redirect all insecure HTTP requests to HTTPS.

If you are following along and hitting a wall, check your IAM policy ARN and Default Root Object first—those are usually the culprits.
